A **real Poisson algebra** is a commutative unital algebra over $\mathbb R$
equipped with an $\mathbb R$-bilinear bracket $\{\ ,\ \}$ that is
skew-symmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity, and is a derivation in each
entry. The algebra-over-a-commutative-ring convention is the one in
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). A **smooth
bivector datum** on $M$ assigns to each smooth coordinate chart
$x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ smooth functions $\pi_x^{ij}$ on its coordinate
domain, with $\pi_x^{ij}=-\pi_x^{ji}$. On an overlap with coordinates
$y=(y^1,\ldots,y^n)$, require the contravariant tensor transformation law
$$\pi_y^{ab}(y(x))= \sum_{i,j=1}^n\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(x) \frac{\partial y^b}{\partial x^j}(x)\pi_x^{ij}(x).$$
For smooth functions $f,g$ on a coordinate domain, the associated local
bracket is
$$\{f,g\}_{\pi,x}:=\sum_{i,j=1}^n\pi_x^{ij}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x^j}.$$
A bivector datum is **Poisson** when this local bracket satisfies the Jacobi
identity on every coordinate domain. A **Poisson manifold** is a smooth
manifold with a Poisson bivector datum. The next proposition proves that the
local brackets agree on overlaps, are biderivations, and satisfy Jacobi
exactly when the Schouten self-bracket vanishes; it justifies this definition
as a global Poisson bracket.

Here $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and repeated coordinate indices
in tensor formulas are summed. To fix the Schouten convention needed here, put
$$J_\pi^{ijk}=\pi^{i\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{jk} +\pi^{j\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ki} +\pi^{k\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ij}.$$
For $\pi=\tfrac12\pi^{ij}\partial_i\wedge\partial_j$, the local
components of its Schouten–Nijenhuis self-bracket are
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}^{ijk}:=2J_\pi^{ijk}$. In this pair,
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}=0$ means that these coefficients vanish in every chart.

No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed on $\pi$. In particular, the zero
bivector and bivectors of nonconstant rank are permitted. No global frame of
the tangent bundle is chosen.
If $F:M\to N$ and $G:N\to P$ are smooth, then $d(G\circ F)_p=dG_{F(p)}\circ dF_p$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: On an overlap, write $J^a_i=\partial y^a/\partial x^i$. By [F2], $\partial_{x^i}f=J^a_i\partial_{y^a}f$ and likewise for $g$. Then [F1] gives $$\pi_x^{ij}(\partial_{x^i}f)(\partial_{x^j}g) =\pi_x^{ij}J^a_iJ^b_j(\partial_{y^a}f)(\partial_{y^b}g) =\pi_y^{ab}(\partial_{y^a}f)(\partial_{y^b}g),$$ so the local bracket is independent of the chart. Skew-symmetry and real-bilinearity follow from $\pi^{ij}=-\pi^{ji}$ and the coordinate formula.

The coordinate product rule gives $\{f,gh\}_{\pi}=\pi^{ij}f_i(g_jh+gh_j) =\{f,g\}_{\pi}h+g\{f,h\}_{\pi}$. Skew-symmetry gives the derivation rule in the first entry as well. Hence the bracket is a biderivation.

In a chart, expand the cyclic Jacobiator $\{f,\{g,h\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi}+\{g,\{h,f\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi} +\{h,\{f,g\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi}$. Its first-derivative terms are $J^{ijk}f_i g_j h_k$. The second-derivative terms cancel in pairs: the terms with $g_{\ell j}$ have coefficients $\pi^{i\ell}\pi^{jk}$ and $\pi^{k\ell}\pi^{ij}$, which cancel after interchanging $j,\ell$ in the second term and using skew-symmetry; the terms with $h_{\ell k}$ cancel after interchanging $\ell,k$; the terms with $f_{\ell i}$ cancel after interchanging $\ell,i$. Thus the displayed Jacobiator formula holds for all smooth $f,g,h$.

If every $J^{ijk}$ vanishes, step 2.2 makes every local Jacobiator zero, so the glued bracket on $C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfies Jacobi. Conversely, assume that global bracket satisfies Jacobi. Fix a point $p$ in a chart $x:U\to x(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and indices $i,j,k$. Choose $0<r<R$ with the closed coordinate ball of radius $R$ about $x(p)$ contained in $x(U)$. Define $\theta(t)=0$ for $t\leq0$ and $\theta(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$, and put
$$\chi(q):=\frac{\theta(R^2-\lVert q-x(p)\rVert^2)}{\theta(R^2-\lVert q-x(p)\rVert^2)+\theta(\lVert q-x(p)\rVert^2-r^2)}.$$
The function $\theta$ is smooth at $0$ because all its right derivatives there tend to zero, and the denominator defining $\chi$ is everywhere positive. Thus $\chi$ is smooth, equals $1$ near $x(p)$, and vanishes outside the closed ball, which is compactly contained in $x(U)$. The functions $f,g,h$ defined on $U$ by $(\chi\circ x)x^i,(\chi\circ x)x^j,(\chi\circ x)x^k$ and extended by zero outside $U$ are therefore smooth global functions and agree with the corresponding coordinates near $p$. By step 2.2 their global Jacobiator at $p$ is $J^{ijk}(p)$, so global Jacobi forces $J^{ijk}(p)=0$. Since $p$ and the indices were arbitrary, every coefficient vanishes in every chart. The Jacobiator is formed from the chart-independent bracket of step 1.1, so the criterion is coordinate-independent. By [F3], the Schouten self-bracket vanishes exactly when these coefficients vanish, since $2$ is invertible over $\mathbb R$. This proves the claimed Poisson and Schouten criteria and justifies the bracket in [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]].

Let $A$ be a commutative unital algebra over $\mathbb R$, with
multiplication $m(f,g)=fg$. Write $A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ for the real formal
power-series module with coefficients in $A$; its underlying coefficient
and Cauchy-product conventions are those of
[[def-formal-power-series-and-coefficient-extraction]]. The $\hbar$-adic
topology is the coefficient-prefix topology of
[[def-formal-order-and-x-adic-topology]]: two series are close modulo
$\hbar^N$ when their coefficients agree in degrees below $N$.

A **formal associative deformation** of $A$ is specified by real-bilinear
maps $B_r:A\times A\to A$ for $r\geq 1$, with $B_0:=m$, and the
product
$$\left(\sum_{i\geq0}\hbar^if_i\right)\star \left(\sum_{j\geq0}\hbar^jg_j\right) =\sum_{N\geq0}\hbar^N\sum_{\substack{i,j,r\geq0\\i+j+r=N}}B_r(f_i,g_j).$$
For each fixed $N$ the inner sum is finite, so this formula defines a
coefficientwise-continuous, $\mathbb R\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$-bilinear product. It is
required to be associative and unital with unit $1$; equivalently,
$B_r(1,f)=B_r(f,1)=0$ for $r\geq1$. Reduction modulo $\hbar$ is the
original product $m$.

This definition alone asserts no differential-order condition, no specified
first-order bracket, no convergence at a numerical value of $\hbar$, and no
existence or classification theorem.

derivations.claim: For any associative product, the commutator $[a,b]_\star=a\star b-b\star a$ satisfies the Jacobi identity. Expanding $[\,[f,g]_\star,k]_\star$ gives $(f\star g)\star k-(g\star f)\star k-k\star(f\star g)+k\star(g\star f)$. After reassociating each term, this is $f\star g\star k-g\star f\star k-k\star f\star g+k\star g\star f$; the two cyclic rotations are $g\star k\star f-k\star g\star f-f\star g\star k+f\star k\star g$ and $k\star f\star g-f\star k\star g-g\star k\star f+g\star f\star k$. Their sum is zero by pairwise cancellation.

Associativity also gives the exact derivation identity $[f,g\star k]_\star=[f,g]_\star\star k+g\star[f,k]_\star$: expanding both sides and reassociating the four triple products leaves the same expression. Comparing coefficients of $\hbar$ gives $\beta(f,gk)=\beta(f,g)k+g\beta(f,k)$.

Since $fg=gf$, the coefficient of $\hbar$ in $[f,g]_\star$ is exactly $\beta(f,g)$. The coefficient of $\hbar^2$ in the commutator Jacobi identity from step 1.1 is $\beta(\beta(f,g),k)+\beta(\beta(g,k),f)+\beta(\beta(k,f),g)=0$. Skew-symmetry of $\beta$ converts this to the Jacobi identity in [F2].

By definition, $\beta$ is real-bilinear and skew-symmetric. The derivation rule in step 1.2 and skew-symmetry give the derivation rule in the first entry; step 2.1 gives Jacobi. These are exactly the Poisson-algebra axioms in [F2].

Let $A$ be a unital associative real algebra. For each integer $p\geq1$,
the **Hochschild $p$-cochains** are
$$C^p(A,A):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(A^{\otimes p},A).$$
The Hochschild differential $\delta:C^p\to C^{p+1}$ is
$$\begin{aligned} (\delta\phi)(a_1,\ldots,a_{p+1})={}&a_1\phi(a_2,\ldots,a_{p+1})\\ &+\sum_{i=1}^{p}(-1)^i\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1},a_i a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{p+1})\\ &+(-1)^{p+1}\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_p)a_{p+1}. \end{aligned}$$
The general cochain-complex convention is degree $+1$ with square-zero
differential ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]); the proposition
[[prop-hochschild-cochains-form-a-differential-graded-lie-algebra]] proves
that this formula has square zero.

A cochain is **normalized** if it vanishes whenever any input is $1$. If
$A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ for a smooth manifold $M$, a cochain is
**multidifferential** if in every coordinate chart it is locally a finite sum
of terms
$$c_{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_p}(x) \prod_{j=1}^{p}\partial^{\alpha_j}f_j(x),$$
with smooth coefficients and a finite order bound in each input. The
normalized multidifferential cochains are the subcomplex used for differential
star-product obstructions; closure under $\delta$ and insertion is proved
in the cited proposition. For $r\geq2$, $HH^r_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}(A,A)$
denotes the kernel of $\delta:C^r_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}\to
C^{r+1}_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}$ modulo the image from degree $r-1$.

For $\phi\in C^p(A,A)$ and $\psi\in C^q(A,A)$, define insertion
$$(\phi\circ\psi)(a_1,\ldots,a_{p+q-1})= \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{(q-1)i} \phi(a_1,\ldots,a_i,\psi(a_{i+1},\ldots,a_{i+q}), a_{i+q+1},\ldots,a_{p+q-1}),$$
and the **Gerstenhaber bracket** by
$$[\phi,\psi]_G:=\phi\circ\psi- (-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)}\psi\circ\phi.$$
The shifted degree of a $p$-cochain is $p-1$. These formulas fix all
insertion signs used in the local deformation equations below.

derivations.claim: Write $\phi\circ_i\psi$ for insertion of a $q$-cochain into slot $i$ of a $p$-cochain, with slots numbered from $0$, so $\phi\circ\psi=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{i(q-1)}\phi\circ_i\psi$. In $(\phi\circ\psi)\circ\chi-\phi\circ(\psi\circ\chi)$, terms where $\chi$ is inserted into the block occupied by $\psi$ cancel. If that block starts at slot $i$ and $\chi$ is inserted into its local slot $s$, the first expression has coefficient $(-1)^{i(q-1)+(i+s)(r-1)}$, while the second has coefficient $(-1)^{i(q+r-2)+s(r-1)}$; these exponents agree. Every remaining term is a pair of insertions into distinct original slots of $\phi$. For original slots $i<j$, the coefficient with $\psi$ inserted first and $\chi$ second is $(-1)^{i(q-1)+(j+q-1)(r-1)}$; with the insertion order swapped it is $(-1)^{j(r-1)+i(q-1)}$. Their ratio is $(-1)^{(q-1)(r-1)}$. The same comparison for $j<i$ puts the earlier insertion first and gives that same ratio. Thus, with $|\psi|=q-1$ and $|\chi|=r-1$, $$\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi) =(-1)^{|\psi||\chi|}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi), \qquad \operatorname{as}(u,v,w):=(u\circ v)\circ w-u\circ(v\circ w).$$
Since $m$ has shifted degree $1$, $$[m,m]_G(a,b,c)=2\bigl((ab)c-a(bc)\bigr)=0$$ by associativity of $A$. Thus $\partial=[m,-]_G$ has degree $+1$.

The bracket is graded skew by its defining formula. Put $e_{uv}=(-1)^{|u||v|}$. Expanding the graded Jacobi identity, the difference between its right and left sides is $$\begin{aligned} &\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi)-e_{\phi\psi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\phi,\chi) +e_{\phi\psi}e_{\phi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\chi,\phi) -e_{\phi\psi}e_{\phi\chi}e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\psi,\phi)\\ &\hspace{2em}{}+e_{\phi\chi}e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\phi,\psi) -e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi). \end{aligned}$$ Step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi)=e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi)$, $\operatorname{as}(\psi,\phi,\chi)=e_{\phi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\chi,\phi)$, and $\operatorname{as}(\chi,\psi,\phi)=e_{\phi\psi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\phi,\psi)$. Substitution cancels the six terms in three pairs, proving graded Jacobi.

Apply the graded Jacobi identity from step 2.1 with the first two entries equal to $m$. It gives $2\partial^2\phi=\bigl[\,[m,m]_G,\phi\bigr]_G=0$, so $\partial^2=0$ over $\mathbb R$. Applying the same identity with entries $m,\phi,\psi$ gives $\partial[\phi,\psi]_G=[\partial\phi,\psi]_G+ (-1)^{|\phi|}[\phi,\partial\psi]_G$. Hence these operations form a differential graded Lie algebra.

Substitute $m$ and $\phi$ into the insertion formula in [F1]. The two outer insertions give $\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_p)a_{p+1}$ and $(-1)^{p-1}a_1\phi(a_2,\ldots,a_{p+1})$. The internal insertions give $-(-1)^{p-1}\sum_{i=1}^{p}(-1)^{i-1} \phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1},a_i a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{p+1})$. Comparing this with the displayed formula for $\delta$ in [F1] gives $\partial\phi=(-1)^{p-1}\delta\phi$. Since $\partial^2=0$, this also proves $\delta^2=0$.

If a normalized cochain is evaluated on a tuple containing $1$, every insertion term vanishes: the unit either enters the inner cochain, which is normalized, or remains an input of the outer one. In $\delta\phi$, the only potentially nonzero terms when $a_j=1$ are the two neighboring products (or the corresponding endpoint product and boundary term); they have identical cochain arguments and opposite signs, so cancel. Finally, finite compositions of local finite-order differential operators remain finite-order differential operators by the product and chain rules. Thus the normalized multidifferential cochains are closed under the differential and the bracket.

derivations.claim: Let $m(f,g)=fg$ and $x=\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}\hbar^rB_r$, so $m+x$ is the truncated product. For arity-two cochains the insertion formula gives $\tfrac12[m+x,m+x]_G(f,g,h)=( (f\star_{<n}g)\star_{<n}h)- f\star_{<n}(g\star_{<n}h)$. Thus its coefficient at order $n$, where there is no $B_n$ term, is precisely the displayed $O_n$; all lower coefficients vanish by the assumed partial associativity. The same insertion formula gives $\tfrac12\sum_{i+j=n}[B_i,B_j]_G=\sum_{i+j=n}B_i\circ B_j=O_n$, because the bracket of two 2-cochains is symmetric.

In the shifted Hochschild DGLA put $R=\partial x+\tfrac12[x,x]_G=\tfrac12[m+x,m+x]_G$; the last equality uses $[m,m]_G=0$. The DGLA identities give the Bianchi identity $$\partial R+[x,R]_G =\tfrac12\partial[x,x]_G+[x,\partial x]_G +\tfrac12[x,[x,x]_G]_G=0.$$ Indeed, the derivation rule and graded skew-symmetry make the first two terms cancel, and graded Jacobi gives $3[x,[x,x]_G]_G=0$, hence the last term vanishes over $\mathbb R$. By step 1.1, $R$ starts at order $\hbar^n$ with coefficient $O_n$, while $x$ starts at order $\hbar$; therefore the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ in the Bianchi identity is $\partial O_n=0$.

By [F3], $\partial$ on 3-cochains is $\delta$, so $\delta O_n=0$. Each summand of $O_n$ is a composition of normalized bidifferential cochains. An input equal to $1$ either makes the inner cochain vanish or remains a unit input of the outer cochain; composition also preserves finite differential order. Thus $O_n$ lies in the stated normalized multidifferential subcomplex.

Add $\hbar^nB_n$ to the truncated product. The order-$n$ terms in its associator that are linear in $B_n$ are $$B_n(f,g)h+B_n(fg,h)-fB_n(g,h)-B_n(f,gh)=-(\delta B_n)(f,g,h).$$ No term quadratic in $B_n$, or involving $B_n$ and a positive-order coefficient, contributes at order $n$, since those terms have order at least $2n$ or $n+1$. Hence the new order-$n$ associator coefficient is $O_n-\delta B_n$.

The lower associator coefficients already vanish. Therefore $\star_{<n}+\hbar^nB_n$ is associative modulo $\hbar^{n+1}$ exactly when $\delta B_n=O_n$. By step 2.2, $O_n$ is a cocycle in the normalized multidifferential complex; such a $B_n$ exists precisely when its cohomology class is zero. For $n=2$, the defining sum has only $(i,j)=(1,1)$, yielding $O_2=\tfrac12[B_1,B_1]_G$. This proves the finite-order criterion without asserting that later obstruction classes vanish.

Let $(M,\pi)$ be a real Poisson manifold as in
[[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]], with its well-defined bracket
from [[prop-coordinate-jacobi-and-schouten-criterion-for-poisson-bivectors]],
and set $A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. A formal associative deformation
$\star$ of $A$ from
[[def-formal-associative-deformation-of-a-commutative-algebra]] is a
**differential star product quantizing $\pi$** if every coefficient
$B_r$ is bidifferential and
$$B_1(f,g)-B_1(g,f)=\{f,g\}_{\pi}\qquad(f,g\in A).$$
Here **bidifferential** means that in every coordinate chart each $B_r$ is
a finite sum of terms $c_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\,\partial^\alpha f\,
\partial^\beta g$, with smooth coefficients and finite differential order
in each input. The normalization fixes the leading commutator to be
$[f,g]_\star=\hbar\{f,g\}_{\pi}$ modulo $\hbar^2$; no factor of
$1/2$ or $i$ is implicit. A convention using $i\hbar$ instead
requires complexified coefficients and is not used here.

The product is interpreted only coefficientwise in the $\hbar$-adic
topology. This definition asserts neither convergence for a numerical
$\hbar$ nor existence, uniqueness, classification, or an operator
quantization for a given Poisson manifold.

Let $\star$ and $\star'$ be differential star products on the same real
Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$, with $A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. They are
**formally gauge equivalent** if there is an invertible
$\mathbb R\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$-linear map $T:A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket\to A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ of the
form
$$T=\operatorname{id}+\sum_{r\geq1}\hbar^rD_r,$$
where each $D_r:A\to A$ is a differential operator and $D_r(1)=0$,
such that
$$f\star' g=T^{-1}\bigl(Tf\star Tg\bigr).$$
The condition $D_r(1)=0$ makes $T(1)=1$, so this change of variables
preserves the unit. The map is formal and coefficientwise; no analytic
convergence or classification of equivalence classes is asserted.

Let $A$ be a unital associative real algebra. For each integer $p\geq1$,
the **Hochschild $p$-cochains** are
$$C^p(A,A):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(A^{\otimes p},A).$$
The Hochschild differential $\delta:C^p\to C^{p+1}$ is
$$\begin{aligned} (\delta\phi)(a_1,\ldots,a_{p+1})={}&a_1\phi(a_2,\ldots,a_{p+1})\\ &+\sum_{i=1}^{p}(-1)^i\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1},a_i a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{p+1})\\ &+(-1)^{p+1}\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_p)a_{p+1}. \end{aligned}$$
The general cochain-complex convention is degree $+1$ with square-zero
differential ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]); the proposition
[[prop-hochschild-cochains-form-a-differential-graded-lie-algebra]] proves
that this formula has square zero.

A cochain is **normalized** if it vanishes whenever any input is $1$. If
$A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ for a smooth manifold $M$, a cochain is
**multidifferential** if in every coordinate chart it is locally a finite sum
of terms
$$c_{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_p}(x) \prod_{j=1}^{p}\partial^{\alpha_j}f_j(x),$$
with smooth coefficients and a finite order bound in each input. The
normalized multidifferential cochains are the subcomplex used for differential
star-product obstructions; closure under $\delta$ and insertion is proved
in the cited proposition. For $r\geq2$, $HH^r_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}(A,A)$
denotes the kernel of $\delta:C^r_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}\to
C^{r+1}_{\mathrm{diff,norm}}$ modulo the image from degree $r-1$.

For $\phi\in C^p(A,A)$ and $\psi\in C^q(A,A)$, define insertion
$$(\phi\circ\psi)(a_1,\ldots,a_{p+q-1})= \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{(q-1)i} \phi(a_1,\ldots,a_i,\psi(a_{i+1},\ldots,a_{i+q}), a_{i+q+1},\ldots,a_{p+q-1}),$$
and the **Gerstenhaber bracket** by
$$[\phi,\psi]_G:=\phi\circ\psi- (-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)}\psi\circ\phi.$$
The shifted degree of a $p$-cochain is $p-1$. These formulas fix all
insertion signs used in the local deformation equations below.

Let $A$ be a unital associative real algebra and use the cochains, standard
Hochschild differential $\delta$, and Gerstenhaber bracket of
[[def-hh-cochain-complex-and-gerstenhaber-bracket]]. Give
$C^p(A,A)$ shifted degree $p-1$, and put
$\partial\phi=[m,\phi]_G$, where $m(a,b)=ab$. Then
$L^j=C^{j+1}(A,A)$, $j\geq0$, is a differential graded Lie algebra:
the bracket has degree zero and satisfies graded skew-symmetry and Jacobi;
$\partial$ has degree $+1$, squares to zero, and obeys
$$\partial[\phi,\psi]_G=[\partial\phi,\psi]_G +(-1)^{|\phi|}[\phi,\partial\psi]_G.$$
For $\phi\in C^p$, $\partial\phi=(-1)^{p-1}\delta\phi$. In particular,
the standard Hochschild cochains form a cochain complex. When
$A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, the normalized multidifferential cochains are
closed under both $\delta$ and $[\ ,\ ]_G$.

Here a differential graded Lie algebra means a graded Lie bracket and a
degree-one square-zero differential satisfying the displayed signed
derivation rule. The base field is $\mathbb R$, so division by $2$ is
valid.

derivations.claim: The coefficient of $\hbar$ in associativity of $\star$ is $B_1(f,g)h+B_1(fg,h)-fB_1(g,h)-B_1(f,gh)=0$, which is $-(\delta B_1)(f,g,h)=0$. The same calculation applies to $\star'$, so both first coefficients are normalized 2-cocycles in the complex of [F4].
Comparing coefficients of $\hbar$ in $TT^{-1}=\operatorname{id}$ gives $T^{-1}=\operatorname{id}-\hbar D_1+O(\hbar^2)$.

Expand the defining transformation from [F2] through first order: $$Tf\star Tg=fg+\hbar\bigl(D_1(f)g+fD_1(g)+B_1(f,g)\bigr) +O(\hbar^2).$$ Applying $T^{-1}$ subtracts $\hbar D_1(fg)$, hence $B_1'=B_1+fD_1(g)-D_1(fg)+D_1(f)g=B_1+\delta D_1$ by [F3].

Since $A$ is commutative, $\delta D_1(f,g)=fD_1(g)-D_1(fg)+D_1(f)g$ equals $\delta D_1(g,f)$. Thus the skew parts of $B_1$ and $B_1'$ agree, and their difference is the coboundary $\delta D_1$. With step 1.1 this proves equality of their classes in the cohomology of [F4].

A **real Poisson algebra** is a commutative unital algebra over $\mathbb R$
equipped with an $\mathbb R$-bilinear bracket $\{\ ,\ \}$ that is
skew-symmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity, and is a derivation in each
entry. The algebra-over-a-commutative-ring convention is the one in
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). A **smooth
bivector datum** on $M$ assigns to each smooth coordinate chart
$x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ smooth functions $\pi_x^{ij}$ on its coordinate
domain, with $\pi_x^{ij}=-\pi_x^{ji}$. On an overlap with coordinates
$y=(y^1,\ldots,y^n)$, require the contravariant tensor transformation law
$$\pi_y^{ab}(y(x))= \sum_{i,j=1}^n\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(x) \frac{\partial y^b}{\partial x^j}(x)\pi_x^{ij}(x).$$
For smooth functions $f,g$ on a coordinate domain, the associated local
bracket is
$$\{f,g\}_{\pi,x}:=\sum_{i,j=1}^n\pi_x^{ij}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x^j}.$$
A bivector datum is **Poisson** when this local bracket satisfies the Jacobi
identity on every coordinate domain. A **Poisson manifold** is a smooth
manifold with a Poisson bivector datum. The next proposition proves that the
local brackets agree on overlaps, are biderivations, and satisfy Jacobi
exactly when the Schouten self-bracket vanishes; it justifies this definition
as a global Poisson bracket.

Here $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and repeated coordinate indices
in tensor formulas are summed. To fix the Schouten convention needed here, put
$$J_\pi^{ijk}=\pi^{i\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{jk} +\pi^{j\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ki} +\pi^{k\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ij}.$$
For $\pi=\tfrac12\pi^{ij}\partial_i\wedge\partial_j$, the local
components of its Schouten–Nijenhuis self-bracket are
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}^{ijk}:=2J_\pi^{ijk}$. In this pair,
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}=0$ means that these coefficients vanish in every chart.

No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed on $\pi$. In particular, the zero
bivector and bivectors of nonconstant rank are permitted. No global frame of
the tangent bundle is chosen.

Let $M$ and $\pi$ be as in
[[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]. The local formulas
$$\{f,g\}_{\pi,x}=\pi_x^{ij}(\partial_i f)(\partial_j g)$$
agree on coordinate overlaps and define a real Poisson-algebra bracket on
$C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ exactly when, in every coordinate chart,
$$J^{ijk}:=\pi^{i\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{jk} +\pi^{j\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ki} +\pi^{k\ell}\partial_\ell\pi^{ij}=0.$$
With the convention $\pi=\tfrac12\pi^{ij}\partial_i\wedge\partial_j$,
the Schouten–Nijenhuis self-bracket has components
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}^{ijk}=2J^{ijk}$. Thus the Jacobi condition is equivalently
$[\pi,\pi]_{SN}=0$. No nondegeneracy or choice axiom is used.

Let $A$ be a commutative unital real algebra and let $\star$ be a formal
associative deformation of $A$ as in
[[def-formal-associative-deformation-of-a-commutative-algebra]]. For
$f,g\in A$, define
$$\beta(f,g):=B_1(f,g)-B_1(g,f).$$
Then $\beta$ is a real Poisson-algebra bracket on $A$. Thus the
first-order skew part of an associative deformation necessarily satisfies
the Lie and biderivation axioms; this is a necessary compatibility statement,
not an existence theorem for a prescribed bracket.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb R^3$ with coordinates $(x,y,z)$, take the smooth bivector $$\pi=x\,\partial_y\wedge\partial_z +y\,\partial_z\wedge\partial_x +xy\,\partial_x\wedge\partial_y.$$ By [F1], its coordinate brackets are $\{y,z\}_\pi=x$, $\{z,x\}_\pi=y$, and $\{x,y\}_\pi=xy$.

Using the biderivation rule, its Jacobiator on these coordinate functions is $$\{\{x,y\}_\pi,z\}_\pi+\{\{y,z\}_\pi,x\}_\pi +\{\{z,x\}_\pi,y\}_\pi =\{xy,z\}_\pi+\{x,x\}_\pi+\{y,y\}_\pi =x^2-y^2.$$ At $(x,y,z)=(1,0,0)$ this is nonzero; by [F2], $\pi$ is not Poisson.

If a unital associative formal deformation had this first-order skew bracket, [F3] would force that bracket to satisfy Jacobi, contradicting step 2.1. Therefore this smooth bivector is not the first-order antisymmetric commutator of any such deformation, refuting the universal claim.

Let $A$ be a commutative unital algebra over $\mathbb R$, with
multiplication $m(f,g)=fg$. Write $A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ for the real formal
power-series module with coefficients in $A$; its underlying coefficient
and Cauchy-product conventions are those of
[[def-formal-power-series-and-coefficient-extraction]]. The $\hbar$-adic
topology is the coefficient-prefix topology of
[[def-formal-order-and-x-adic-topology]]: two series are close modulo
$\hbar^N$ when their coefficients agree in degrees below $N$.

A **formal associative deformation** of $A$ is specified by real-bilinear
maps $B_r:A\times A\to A$ for $r\geq 1$, with $B_0:=m$, and the
product
$$\left(\sum_{i\geq0}\hbar^if_i\right)\star \left(\sum_{j\geq0}\hbar^jg_j\right) =\sum_{N\geq0}\hbar^N\sum_{\substack{i,j,r\geq0\\i+j+r=N}}B_r(f_i,g_j).$$
For each fixed $N$ the inner sum is finite, so this formula defines a
coefficientwise-continuous, $\mathbb R\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$-bilinear product. It is
required to be associative and unital with unit $1$; equivalently,
$B_r(1,f)=B_r(f,1)=0$ for $r\geq1$. Reduction modulo $\hbar$ is the
original product $m$.

This definition alone asserts no differential-order condition, no specified
first-order bracket, no convergence at a numerical value of $\hbar$, and no
existence or classification theorem.

from [[prop-coordinate-jacobi-and-schouten-criterion-for-poisson-bivectors]],

$\star$ of $A$ from

**differential star product quantizing $\pi$** if every coefficient
$B_r$ is bidifferential and
$$B_1(f,g)-B_1(g,f)=\{f,g\}_{\pi}\qquad(f,g\in A).$$

in each input. The normalization fixes the leading commutator to be

topology. This definition asserts neither convergence for a numerical

quantization for a given Poisson manifold.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

For $F,G\in C^\infty(M)$, the **Poisson bracket** in the library convention is

$$\{F,G\}:=\omega(X_F,X_G)=dF(X_G)=X_G(F)=-X_F(G).$$

All four formulas use $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. In particular, the order in the
observable formula is important: evolution by $H$ differentiates $F$ as
$X_H(F)=\{F,H\}$.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

derivations.claim: Since $\Pi^{ij}$ is constant, every derivative in [F2] is zero, so its Jacobiator vanishes. Thus [F1] gives a Poisson bracket for every constant skew matrix, with no rank assumption.

On $\mathbb R^{2n}$, $\omega=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ is closed because $$d\omega=\sum_i d(dq^i\wedge dp_i)=\sum_i(d^2q^i\wedge dp_i-dq^i\wedge d^2p_i)=0.$$ For $X=\sum_i(a_i\partial_{q^i}+b_i\partial_{p_i})$, $\iota_X\omega=\sum_i(a_i\,dp_i-b_i\,dq^i)$; if this vanishes then every $a_i=b_i=0$, so it is pointwise nondegenerate and is symplectic by [F7]. Equating $\iota_{X_H}\omega$ with $dH=\sum_i(H_{q^i}\,dq^i+H_{p_i}\,dp_i)$, [F5] gives $X_H=\sum_i(H_{p_i}\partial_{q^i}-H_{q^i}\partial_{p_i})$. Therefore $X_G(F)=\sum_i(F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i})$ by [F6], exactly the bracket of [F1] for $\Pi=\sum_i\partial_{q^i}\wedge\partial_{p_i}$.

The zeroth exponential term is $fg$, so $B_0=m$. For $r\geq1$, expanding the formal exponential gives $$B_r(f,g)=\frac{1}{2^r r!}\sum_{i_1,j_1,\ldots,i_r,j_r} \Pi^{i_1j_1}\cdots\Pi^{i_rj_r} (\partial_{i_1}\cdots\partial_{i_r}f) (\partial_{j_1}\cdots\partial_{j_r}g).$$ Each coefficient is a finite bidifferential expression. If either input is $1$, every positive-order term vanishes, so the unit is preserved; the series is well-defined coefficientwise by [F3].

On three independent tensor factors define $P_{ab}=\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}\partial_{x_a^i}\otimes\partial_{x_b^j}$ for $1\leq a<b\leq3$, with each operator acting as the identity on the remaining factor, and define $\mu_3(f\otimes g\otimes h)=fgh$. These operators commute because they are sums of products of commuting partial derivatives with constant coefficients. The product rule says that differentiation of the first composite factor is $\partial^{(1)}+\partial^{(2)}$, so $$(f\star g)\star h= \mu_3 e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{13}+P_{23})} e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}P_{12}}(f\otimes g\otimes h),$$ while differentiating the second composite factor gives $$f\star(g\star h)= \mu_3 e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{12}+P_{13})} e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}P_{23}}(f\otimes g\otimes h).$$ For commuting operators $U,V$, the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ in $e^{\hbar U/2}e^{\hbar V/2}$ is $2^{-n}\sum_{r+s=n}U^rV^s/(r!s!)=2^{-n}(U+V)^n/n!$ by the binomial theorem. This is a finite identity at each order, so it applies coefficientwise to these formal exponentials. Commutativity of the three operators makes both expressions $\mu_3e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{12}+P_{13}+P_{23})} (f\otimes g\otimes h)$, proving associativity coefficientwise.

The first coefficient is $B_1(f,g)=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}f_i g_j$. Skew-symmetry of $\Pi$ gives $B_1(f,g)-B_1(g,f)=\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}f_i g_j=\{f,g\}_\Pi$. Hence the product in this example satisfies the first-order normalization in [F4]. When $\Pi=0$, every $P_{ab}=0$ and the product is the ordinary commutative product; no rank or nondegeneracy assumption is needed.
